newsitem.title: SPAIN: BCH says rate cut confirms Spain reaching EMU goal.
newsitem.headline: BCH says rate cut confirms Spain reaching EMU goal.

text.p: The Bank of Spain's move on Friday to lower its key money market rate for the seventh time this year shows the central bank is confident Spain will meet Economic and Monetary Union criteria, BCH analysts said.
Banco Central Hispano-BCH said the new rate cut from 6.75 percent to 6.25 percent was principally due to a favourable inflation trend that the bank said would continue into 1997.

November's consumer price index (CPI) was better than expected by the market and BCH, with the year-on-year rate falling from 3.5 percent to 3.2 percent. The bank said CPI could drop to below 2.5 percent next year.
BCH also forecast the Bank of Spain would keep cutting its key money rate through to the end of 1997, when it would reach 5.5 percent with a 75 basis point spread over the German rate.

"Most of the determining factors for inflation are progressing favourably," BCH said in a statement, listing as reasons: tight fiscal policy, moderate growth in monetary factors, a lack of demand pressures, peseta strength, falling import prices and easing industrial prices.
BCH said the biggest risk to inflation, excessive salary hikes, had been avoided by the government's planned wage freeze for the public sector, which usually guides the private sector.
In addition, year-end inflation for 1996 was now seen down at 3.2 percent, meaning inflation-linked salaries and pensions would be kept down as well.

The bank said there were other factors lending credibility to Spain's bid for the EMU, including increased pressure on the peseta by foreign buying -- an indication of growing confidence the Mediterranean countries would join the single currency.

The Bank of Spain's slow, gradual narrowing of the interest rate spread over other European countries and the ease with which the Treasury was meeting expenses were also cited by BCH as signs Spain was closing in on the EMU criteria.
